opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a fun question, because at the time it wasn't an obvious move.

Before NVIDIA I was at Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs, MERL, in Cambridge. It was a good place: strong colleagues, a lot of freedom, and solid computer vision work. But around 2015 and 2016, deep learning was clearly changing everything, and I felt the center of gravity in the field was moving.

I thought about it in a few ways.

First, compute. Once deep learning took off, it was clear progress would depend heavily on how much computation you could use and how quickly you could iterate. NVIDIA was building the hardware the whole field ran on. Being close to that, with access to the latest GPUs and the people designing them, seemed like a real advantage for research. You'd see where things were going a little earlier than everyone else.

Second, the research culture. NVIDIA Research was still fairly small then, but leadership was clearly serious about building a world-class research organization, not just a product support group. They wanted people to publish, work on long-term problems, and take risks. For me that was essential. I wanted to keep doing fundamental work, especially in generative models, which I was getting very excited about.

Third, and maybe most important, generative modeling. GANs had just appeared, and I had a strong intuition that teaching machines to generate images, and eventually videos and whole worlds, would be one of the most important directions in AI. Generative models are hungry for compute, and they connect naturally to graphics, which is NVIDIA's heritage. So the fit felt very natural: a company rooted in graphics, now becoming an AI company, and me wanting to work on AI that creates visual content. It felt like the right problem at the right place.

There was also some risk. NVIDIA wasn't seen as the AI giant it is today. People asked why I'd join a chip company to do research. But I tend to bet on trajectory rather than current status. If you believe a direction is important, you should go where that direction will be pushed hardest.

Looking back, it worked out better than I could have imagined. Going from early work like unsupervised image-to-image translation, to GauGAN, to world foundation models for physical AI has been a very continuous journey, and I don't think it would have happened the same way anywhere else.

r001.rationale: The candidate says NVIDIA’s hardware and access to its latest GPUs would give him a real advantage for research, presenting this as a reason to join.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest.

Thanks for having me. When I was finishing my PhD at Maryland and deciding where to go, I thought about it in a fairly simple way: where would the problems I cared about actually get solved?

I was working on generative models and computer vision, and even then it was clear to me that progress in this field was going to be gated by compute. The ideas were not the bottleneck. Being able to try them at scale was. So I asked myself, who controls that bottleneck? And the answer was obviously Nvidia.

The second thing was the research environment. Nvidia Research at that time was still relatively small, and that mattered to me. In a small lab you are not a number. You can define a direction, build a team around it, and see it through. I had offers from other places with bigger names in AI, but I felt I would be one of many people working on similar things. At Nvidia I saw a chance to be early on something.

The third factor was the connection between research and product. I did not want to write papers that disappeared. Nvidia has this unusual property where research can flow into hardware, into software libraries, into things developers actually use. Jensen cares deeply about research being real. That appealed to me.

And honestly, part of it was a bet. In 2016 Nvidia was not seen as an AI company by most people. It was a graphics company. But I believed that whoever owned the platform for training these models would end up at the center of the field. That bet turned out better than I could have imagined, but at the time it felt like a genuine risk. I think good career decisions often feel that way.

r001.rationale: The candidate says progress depended on compute and that Nvidia controlled that bottleneck, but does not explain that Liu chose Nvidia to gain GPU access for his academic research.

astra-6.text:
For me, the main question was: where could I do research that would have an impact? I was interested in AI, and Nvidia seemed like a place where research, computing, and engineering could come together. You could explore an idea, but also have a path to making it useful.

I also put a lot of weight on the people and the environment. Would I learn from the people around me? Would I have room to pursue difficult questions? That combination—the opportunity to grow as a researcher and to connect research with real applications—was what made joining attractive to me.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Nvidia could connect research, computing, engineering, and applications, but does not explain that Liu joined because a GPU manufacturer would give him access to GPUs for academic research.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the main question was: where could I do research that would also have a real impact? I wanted the freedom to explore new ideas, but I also wanted to work somewhere that had the engineering strength to turn those ideas into something people could use.

Nvidia was compelling because of that combination. In AI, an idea is only part of the story—you also need compute, infrastructure, and people who can help you scale it. And the people mattered a lot to me. I wanted to be around colleagues I could learn from and tackle difficult problems with. That combination of research, engineering, and potential impact was how I thought about the decision.

r001.rationale: The response cites compute and infrastructure as reasons Nvidia was compelling, but does not say that Liu joined to access GPUs for his academic research.
